Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

apaTables 4.0.0

This release follows 2.0.8, the previous version on CRAN, so everything below describes what changed for someone upgrading from that version. Versions 3.0.0 and 3.0.1 existed on GitHub only and were never released.

apaquarto / Quarto support

  • apaTables now ships a patched copy of the apaquarto Quarto extension and can install it for you, rather than asking you to run the Quarto extension commands. apa.quarto.new(path = "my-paper") creates a folder containing a Quarto document with a working APA header and a worked table, with the extension already installed beside it, so the very first render produces a real APA manuscript. apa.quarto.setup() installs or repairs the extension in a project you already have, and is silent when the project’s copy is already correct. Running quarto add wjschne/apaquarto or quarto update extension wjschne/apaquarto in one of these projects silently reverts the extension to the stock, unpatched copy – while reporting [No Change] – undoing the fixes; running apa.quarto.setup() again puts the tested copy back.
  • In an apaquarto PDF, a document containing tables written as plain markdown now numbers every table 1, 2, 3, … and its cross-references match. With the stock extension under Quarto 1.9, each markdown table is captioned “Table 1” and every reference to one reads “Table 1”; in a document that mixes markdown tables with apaTables tables, the apaTables table after each markdown table repeats its number instead. The bundled extension carries the fix.
  • In an apaquarto Word or HTML document, markdown tables whose labels share a first part – {#tbl-md-plain} and {#tbl-md-note}, or {#tbl-a_b} and {#tbl-a_c}, say – number 1, 2, 3, … like any others, and their cross-references match. With the stock extension such tables are captioned with the same number, because each label was read only up to the first hyphen, underscore, dot or colon after tbl-. The bundled extension carries the fix.
  • In an apaquarto PDF, a long table written in markdown, or made by knitr::kable() in a chunk with a tbl-cap, continues onto the next page with every row, prints its caption once, and keeps its note with it when tables are collected at the end of the manuscript. With the stock extension under Quarto 1.9 such a table stops at the foot of its first page and every later row is lost, with no error or warning. (Journal mode, documentmode: jou, still cannot break a table across pages.)
  • In an apaquarto PDF the rows of apaTables’ tables, markdown tables and knitr::kable() tables are single-spaced, as in Word, and a table’s note keeps the manuscript’s spacing, as in Word. Each such table closes with a single bottom rule (with the stock extension a markdown table without a caption ends with two), and a table’s note is kept on a page with at least one of its rows unless the note itself is longer than about a quarter of a page.
  • An apaquarto PDF with line numbers (numbered-lines: true) renders when it contains tables: the text around each table is numbered and the rows of the table are not. With the stock extension, a captioned table set to break across pages (apa-longtable: true) stops the render with “Undefined control sequence”, and so does an uncaptioned table whose first cell spans columns (\multicolumn). The bundled extension sets every apaTables table and every captioned markdown table that way, so without the fix a line-numbered manuscript with almost any table would not render.
  • In an apaquarto PDF, a table written as raw LaTeX, by knitr::kable(format = "latex") or kableExtra, in a chunk with a tbl-cap, prints like any other table: its title sits above the top rule and its note below the bottom rule, it stays where it was written in the text, and a long one continues onto the next page with every row, its column headings repeated and its note at the end. (Two cases still print as before: kableExtra’s latex_options = "scale_down", and a caption given to kable(caption = ...) itself rather than with tbl-cap.) With the stock extension the title is struck through by the top rule, “Note.” prints over the last row, in documentmode: doc the table drifts away from where it was written, and a long one is cut off at the foot of the page with its note.
  • Tables drop directly into apaquarto documents. Build the table on one line and pass it to the entry point named for the output format on the next: apa.quarto.pdf(), apa.quarto.docx(), apa.quarto.html() or apa.quarto.revealjs(). The same analysis produces a PDF, a Word file, a web page or a slide – you change the document’s format: line and the matching call, not your code.
  • The table’s number, title and note are supplied automatically. Nothing has to be typed for them, and they are re-derived on every render, so they stay correct when the analysis changes. To use your own wording instead, add a tbl-cap or apa-note chunk option, or pass title = / note = to the entry point; whichever is supplied wins over the generated version, and the chunk option wins over the argument. apa.caption() and apa.note.text() return the apaTables wording for an author who would rather start from it.
  • apa.quarto.template(), run in the R console, prints a ready-to-paste block of code for a table you have already built. It derives the chunk label from the name you typed – apa.quarto.template(x = table3) labels the chunk tbl-table3 – so two templates pasted into one document do not collide.
  • Wide and tall tables are handled without anything being added to the document. apaTables measures each table as the document renders and asks apaquarto for a rotated (landscape) page when it will not stand upright, at full size, under either table placement. A table taller than the page continues onto the next one with its column headings repeated. Every table function takes a landscape argument for the cases where you want to overrule the measurement: TRUE forces a rotated page, FALSE forbids one, and the default measures. The chunk option #| apa-landscape: overrides that argument and can also forbid one.
  • The Quarto entry points take a font.size argument, and it means the same thing on all four destinations: your size exactly, applied to the table body. Where a destination cannot deliver the size asked for, it says so in the rendered draft. Word’s range is 6 to 12 pt.
  • In Word output, the automatic fit counts the fixed padding every Word table cell carries (which does not shrink with the type, so it weighs most on dense tables at small sizes), so a many-column table is set at a size that keeps every label on one line.
  • The page a table is fitted to is read from the settings in the document rather than assumed: US letter and A4 paper and a geometry: margin= setting are recognized. When the YAML carries something apaTables cannot measure, the standard manuscript page is used and the knitted draft says so.
  • New apa.quarto.example() writes two ready-to-edit example documents that demonstrate every table type, one table per page – one document per common destination: <name>-pdf.qmd renders to a PDF manuscript and <name>-docx.qmd to a Word manuscript. Both use the apaquarto extension, which the function installs alongside them. It returns their paths invisibly as the named character vector c(pdf = , docx = ). (Using apaTables tables in an ordinary Quarto document without apaquarto is still supported and is covered in the vignette.)
  • Quarto slide support is reveal.js only. apa.quarto.revealjs() fits the table to the slide. PowerPoint is not yet supported: a pptx render still produces the table and warns you, so a deck is never handed out without your knowing.
  • Journal mode (documentmode: jou) is not supported for apaTables tables. A two-column page cannot break a table across pages, so rows, columns and whole notes can be missing, or the render can stop with a LaTeX error and write no PDF. When the PDF does render, apaTables puts a warning in it; use documentmode: man, or save the table with apa.save().

File output

  • Table numbers are now real by default. table.number defaults to 1, so a table built without one is Table 1; version 2.0.8 defaulted to NA, which showed no number at the console and wrote “Table XX” in the file. Setting table.number = 0 – or NA, or NULL – now means the table carries no number at all: none is shown at the console or written to the Word file. When apa.save() writes several tables to one file, a number you supplied is kept, and a table left at the default takes the next number after the last numbered table before it, starting at 1 (three defaults give Table 1, 2, 3; a supplied 5 in the middle gives Table 1, 5, 6). In an apaquarto document the value is ignored, because apaquarto numbers the tables itself.
  • New apa.save() writes one or more tables to a Microsoft Word .docx or an .html file (chosen by file extension) via flextable/officer. A table function’s filename = argument writes the same files: the hand-rolled RTF engine of 2.0.8 has been retired, so a .doc/.rtf filename is written as .docx, and any other ending stops with an error. apa.save() does not write PDF; for a PDF table, use apa.quarto.pdf() inside an apaquarto / Quarto document, which is what the error message says if you try.
  • Every table function now takes a landscape argument, and it is a three-way setting rather than an on/off switch: TRUE forces a rotated page, FALSE forbids one, and the default – NA – measures the table and decides. This changes existing behavior: in 2.0.8 apa.cor.table(), apa.d.table() and apa.2way.table() defaulted to landscape = TRUE and apa.reg.table() always wrote a landscape page, so those tables were rotated whether or not they needed it. Nothing rotates now unless it does not fit. Pass landscape = TRUE for the old orientation.
  • apa.afex.table() is new: an APA ANOVA table from afex::aov_ez() output, covering the repeated-measures and mixed designs apa.ezANOVA.table() used to serve. Its table.title argument is honored in every destination, and “ANOVA Results” is the title when none is given.
  • .html output from apa.save() carries the same APA elements as the Word file: the table’s caption holds the “Table N” line and the italic title, and the note sits below the table, with its italics and super/subscripts intact. Table numbers are assigned exactly as for .docx, so the same tables saved to both formats carry the same numbers. Writing .html needs pandoc; without it apa.save() stops with a message that says so and points to .docx, which does not need pandoc.
  • Tables are left-aligned so each shares the same left margin as its number, title, and note. Correlation and d-value tables add a blank line of separation between variable rows for readability.
  • Word output follows APA 7 table setup: the table number is bold, the title sits one double-spaced line below it, and a blank line separates the table from its note. The note preserves italics and super/subscripts (e.g., M, SD, eta-squared symbols), and the significance-star sentence (“* indicates p < .05. ** indicates p < .01.”) starts on a new line. Regression Fit cells render R-squared and change-in-R-squared with proper italics, superscripts, and the Delta symbol. Table pages use 0.5 in side margins, and a table wider than the text area is scaled to fit it rather than clipped by Word.
  • Notes keep their styling in every destination – italic M, subscripts and superscripts, and a multi-part note that starts each part, such as the significance-star sentence, on a new line.

Deprecations and dependencies

  • Breaking: apa.ezANOVA.table() has been removed. The ez package it depended on was archived on CRAN; use apa.afex.table() with afex::aov_ez() output for repeated-measures and mixed designs instead.

  • Breaking: apa.reg.boot.table() has been removed. Bootstrapped regression tables are not part of this release; use apa.reg.table() for the standard regression table.

  • apa.knit.table.for.pdf() and apa.knit.table.for.papaja(), which appeared only in the unreleased 3.0 versions below, are not in this release; apa.quarto.pdf() in an apaquarto document and apa.save() replace them.

  • Correlation tables print each correlation’s p value on a line below its confidence interval (show.pvalue = FALSE gives the 2.0.8 layout), and gain an N column. When the data have missing values, the note also gives the range of the number of cases behind each correlation (pairwise deletion).

  • d-value and one-way tables gain an n column: the number of cases in each group.

  • Settings are checked, and a value that is not allowed stops with a message naming the values that are: conf.level in apa.aov.table() and prop.var.conf.level in apa.reg.table() must be .90 or .95 (2.0.8 silently used .90 and .95, respectively, in place of any other value); landscape must be TRUE, FALSE or NA; and table.number must be a whole number, 0 or more.

  • apa.reg.table() and apa.aov.table() stop with a message for a model with an offset (an offset() term, or the offset argument of lm()). 2.0.8’s apa.reg.table() printed the offset as a predictor row with no estimate, and R-squared is then not the usual proportion of variance explained; apa.aov.table() refuses such models too.

  • The object a table function returns uses the same field names for every table type: table_number, table_title, table_body and table_note. In 2.0.8, correlation, d-value, one-way and two-way tables used table.number, table.title, table.body and table.note and the class apa.table; the class is now apa_table throughout. A regression table’s sr2 and sr2_95%_CI columns are now Unique_R2 and Unique_95%_CI. Titles and notes are generated in APA title case.

  • A regression table labels each predictor row with the term as summary() prints it, with three changes: a product such as I(wt * qsec) reads wt x qsec (2.0.8 printed I(wt * qsec)), a term such as I(wt^2) loses the wrapper (wt^2), and names have no backticks. A factor level prints as R gives it (agegrp26-35).

  • Dependencies have changed. R 4.1.0 or later is required (2.0.8 needed R 3.1.2). boot, tibble and methods are no longer imported (boot and tibble are unused). flextable and officer are new imports, used by apa.save() to write the Word and HTML files, and knitr, which 2.0.8 suggested, is now imported. MBESS stays a required import, as in 2.0.8: it computes the confidence intervals for d values, R-squared and partial eta-squared, so every installation of apaTables prints them.

  • On a Mac without XQuartz, some builds of gdtools (a package flextable needs) cannot load – Posit Package Manager’s can fail this way; CRAN’s do not. apa.save() and the Quarto entry points now stop with a message that says how to fix it (install XQuartz, or reinstall gdtools from CRAN) instead of a low-level library-loading error.

Bug fixes

  • apa.aov.table() now gives correct Type III main effects whatever contrasts the model was fitted with. Under R’s default treatment contrasts, a factor’s row in a model with an interaction was the effect at one level of the other factor rather than its main effect, and nothing said so (for the goggles example, alcohol printed as F = 0.61, p = .546 instead of F = 20.07, p < .001). For type = 3, apa.aov.table() now refits the model with sum-to-zero contrasts, as SPSS does, so the table is the same whether or not you set options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")). The refit uses the data stored in the model object, so the table always describes the model you fitted, even if the data in your workspace has changed since. The (Intercept) row printed at the console now tests the grand mean in every case.
  • apa.aov.table(type = 2) left the confidence interval for the first effect blank.
  • apa.aov.table() rounded the sums of squares and F to two decimals before computing the mean squares, partial eta-squared and its confidence interval. For a dependent variable on a very small scale (such as seconds divided by 1000) every sum of squares rounded to zero and partial eta-squared printed as NaN. On a proportion scale partial eta-squared could be .01 off with nothing to show it, and on any scale a mean square or a confidence-interval limit could be .01 off. Everything is now computed at full precision and rounded only when printed.
  • apa.reg.table() accepted blocks that share no predictor, and printed a negative change in R-squared with a [NaN, NaN] interval under a hierarchical title. Each block must now contain every term of the block before it, interactions included, plus at least one more; a step written as a new parameterization, such as wt followed by poly(wt, 2), is still accepted. Blocks must also be fitted to the same cases in the same order, with the same weights. Blocks fitted to different rows (usually because a later predictor has missing values) now stop with a message that shows how to fit every block to the same rows, instead of an error from inside base R.
  • apa.d.table() reports a d-value for every pair of groups. 2.0.8 left the d-value and the interval for it blank when Levene’s test (centered on the median) gave p < .05, and the help page did not say a test made the decision. Every d-value now uses the pooled standard deviation, no test of equal variances is run, and the note says that the d-values use the pooled standard deviation. The note also says that d-values are absolute, so the direction of a difference is read from the means.
  • apa.2way.table() leaves out a case with a missing value on either factor or on the dependent variable from the marginal means, as it already did from the cells. 2.0.8 counted a case missing one factor in the marginal mean of the other, so a marginal mean could differ from the cells beside it.
  • apa.reg.table() leaves out the r column for a weighted model, as 2.0.8 already left out beta. 2.0.8 printed the unweighted correlation there, beside the weighted b, semi-partial correlation squared and R-squared. A table for weighted models no longer stops with an R error when a later block adds a factor predictor or an interaction written a * b or a:b.
  • apa.reg.table() shows the beta and r columns when R writes a predictor name in backticks, as it does for a name with a space or a hyphen (`pre-test`). 2.0.8 left both columns out of the whole table for such a name without saying why; in a table with several blocks, the note still defined them. The name now prints without the backticks. A variable with * or : in the name is no longer taken for a product term, so the r for it is shown.
  • apa.reg.table() no longer stops with an R error (“numbers of columns of arguments do not match”) when an earlier block cannot show beta and r and a later block can – for example, an interaction written wt * qsec in block 1 and I(wt * qsec) in block 2. As the help page says, beta and r are then left out of every block.
  • apa.reg.table() shows an unordered categorical predictor with each level compared with the first level even when options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")) was set before the model was fitted, as is common for an ANOVA. 2.0.8 used the sum-to-zero coding that line sets: the rows read factor(cyl)1, factor(cyl)2, and each b compared one group with the mean of the group means, with nothing in the table to say so. In lm(mpg ~ factor(cyl) + wt, data = mtcars), 6 cylinders printed as -0.81 (not significant) instead of -4.26 (p < .01). Coding chosen for one model is kept when it is dummy coding (such as contr.SAS); other coding, such as effect coding, stops with a message.
  • A p value of exactly .01 is now marked with one significance star. In 2.0.8 it was unmarked; one star was given only for .01 < p < .05.
  • The confidence intervals for the semi-partial correlation squared of each predictor and for the change in R-squared are held to the range 0 to 1. The asymptotic method used for them could print a negative lower limit for a proportion of variance.
  • The two-way table note no longer says that the marginal means pertain to main effects. They are the observed means at each level of a factor; in an unbalanced design these differ from the unweighted means a Type III test compares.
  • Building a d-value table no longer disables warnings for the rest of the session. MBESS::ci.smd() sets options(warn = -1) and does not restore it, so after one apa.d.table() call every later warning – from any package – was discarded; inside a Quarto render that included the apaTables too-wide-table warning. apaTables now saves and restores the option around each call to MBESS.
  • Common input mistakes now stop with a message that says what to change, instead of an error from inside R: a dv that is not numeric; a group, or a cell of a two-way table, with fewer than two cases (the message names it); a correlation table with fewer than two numeric columns, or a column with only one value; a model from glm() given to apa.reg.table() or apa.aov.table(), or no model given to apa.reg.table(); a regression model with no predictor or no intercept; a show/hide argument that is not TRUE or FALSE; and a filename that is not one name. filename = NULL now means no file, as NA does.
  • A grouping variable with unused factor levels, as is common after subset(), now gives a table: the unused levels are left out. 2.0.8 stopped with an error.
  • Printing a table returns the table invisibly, as print() methods do, instead of NULL.

apaTables 3.0

New features

  • Support for latex tables via the new command apa.knit.table.for.pdf()
